analysis.one_liner: Bans medical bills from credit reports and stops lenders from using them.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: after being referred to the Senate Banking Committee in October 2023, it received no further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that medical debt — including medical bills sent to collection agencies — could not appear on anyone's credit report. It would also require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to change its rules so that lenders could not obtain or use a person's medical debt when deciding whether to approve a loan or a credit card.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans who carry medical debt would benefit. Because a medical bill — even one they are disputing, or got while uninsured — can lower a credit score, keeping medical debt off credit reports would protect credit scores for people who got sick, and prevent lenders from treating an illness as a sign of financial risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills on their credit

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines medical debt and adds it to the list of adverse information that consumer reporting agencies are barred from including on a consumer report, covering even medical debt placed for collection or charged off [S3].

It requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, within one year of enactment, to change its regulations so creditors cannot obtain or use medical debt information when deciding whether to extend credit [S3].

The CRS summary states the bill prohibits consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt on consumer reports and directs the CFPB to bar creditors from using medical debt information in credit decisions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting bureaus, medical debt collection agencies, and lenders would lose a widely used data point. Collections agencies would lose the leverage of credit-report threats when trying to collect medical bills, and lenders would lose the ability to screen applicants using medical debt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and medical debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that credit scores are meant to predict whether a borrower will repay; removing medical debt from reports and barring lenders from considering it could raise lending risk for creditors, some of whom argue costs could be passed to other borrowers through pricing (a general mechanism of credit underwriting, not a claim in the provided sources).
The bill only addresses the credit-reporting and lending side of medical debt; it does not reduce, forgive, or lower any medical bills themselves, so the underlying debt would remain owed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to ordinary people is straightforward: medical debt is different from other debt because it often comes from an emergency rather than a borrowing choice, and the bill would stop it from damaging credit or triggering lender screens. The costs fall on the credit-reporting and collections industries and add some underwriting risk for lenders. The bill's main limit is that it treats the symptom — credit damage — not the size of the bills themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in October 2023, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended, so it never received a vote in the Senate or the House.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2023 on October 19, 2023, with Sens. Menendez, Fetterman, and Blumenthal as original cosponsors [S3].
After being read twice, the bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S1].
The complete action history shows no action beyond that referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The bill had four Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting bureaus, medical debt collection agencies, and lenders that use medical debt in underwriting are better off, because the rules the bill would have imposed never took effect. People with medical debt on their credit reports gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats (the sponsor plus four Democratic cosponsors) and no Republicans signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so the full chamber's split was never recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar medical debt — including debt in collections — from credit reports, removing a category of adverse information these companies sell to lenders. Medical debt is a common entry point into the credit reporting system, so the exclusion would shrink the data their scores are built on [S3].

Collectors rely heavily on the threat of credit reporting to push people to pay medical bills; the bill would eliminate that tool, weakening their leverage over millions of consumers with unpaid medical balances [S3].

The bill would prohibit lenders from obtaining or using medical debt information in credit decisions, removing a screening data point. Some lenders argue medical debt predicts repayment; others have moved away from using it. The direct effect is the loss of information they currently may use [S3].
